toLevel2.stem: What does the x-axis of a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve represent?
distractors: Temperature
Concentration
Time

toLevel2.stem: What does the y-axis of a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve represent?
toLevel2.answer: Proportion of molecules with that energy
distractors: Total kinetic energy of all particles
Rate of the chemical reaction
Activation energy of the reaction

toLevel2.stem: What does the area under a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve represent?
distractors: The activation energy of the reaction
The rate of the chemical reaction
The temperature of the system

toLevel2.stem: The shape of a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve starts at zero, rises to a peak, and then:
distractors: drops sharply to zero
continues to rise indefinitely
forms a symmetrical bell shape

toLevel2.stem: Why does the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve never touch the x-axis on the right side?
toLevel2.answer: Some particles always have very high kinetic energy
distractors: The curve is drawn incorrectly if it approaches the axis
All particles have identical kinetic energies
The x-axis represents temperature, not energy

toLevel2.stem: The x-axis of a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve represents kinetic energy and the y-axis represents the proportion of molecules.
distractors: False

toLevel2.stem: A Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve is symmetrical like a normal bell curve.
distractors: True

toLevel3.stem: Why does the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve start at zero on the y-axis?
toLevel3.answer: No particles have zero kinetic energy — all particles are in motion
distractors: The measuring equipment cannot detect particles at zero energy
Zero energy particles are too heavy to be included in the curve
The curve always starts at the activation energy value

toLevel3.stem: Why is the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve asymmetric, with a longer tail to the right?
toLevel3.answer: There is no upper limit to kinetic energy, but there is a lower limit of zero
distractors: The curve is drawn incorrectly and should be perfectly symmetrical
The right side represents particles that have already reacted
The tail represents particles that are not part of the sample

toLevel3.stem: What does the peak of the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve tell us?
toLevel3.answer: The most common kinetic energy among the particles
distractors: The activation energy of the chemical reaction
The temperature of the particle sample
The rate of the reaction at that energy

toLevel3.stem: Why is it important to understand the shape and features of the curve before using it to explain temperature and catalyst effects?
toLevel3.answer: Misinterpreting the axes or shape leads to incorrect explanations of rate changes
distractors: The curve has no connection to temperature or catalyst effects at all
Understanding the shape is only needed for drawing, not for explanations
The shape changes randomly and cannot be predicted in advance

toLevel3.stem: Why does the right tail of the curve extend far along the x-axis?
toLevel3.answer: A small number of particles always have very high kinetic energies
distractors: Those particles have been heated by an external energy source
The tail represents particles that are no longer part of the system
The x-axis scale is compressed on the right side of the diagram

toLevel3.stem: Why does the total area under the curve remain constant at a given temperature?
toLevel3.answer: The total number of particles in the sample does not change
distractors: Energy is conserved so the area must stay the same as energy
The curve is always drawn to the same scale on every diagram
The temperature prevents any change in the area value

toLevel3.stem: The peak of the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve represents the most common kinetic energy among particles in the sample.
distractors: False

toLevel3.stem: The curve is asymmetric because kinetic energy has a lower limit of {{blank:1}} but no upper {{blank:2}}.
distractors: one

toLevel3.stem: The peak of the curve represents the {{blank:1}} common kinetic energy, also called the {{blank:2}} energy.
distractors: least
average

toLevel3.stem: The total area under the curve stays constant because the total number of {{blank:1}} does not {{blank:2}}.
distractors: collisions

toLevel4.stem: A student draws a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve that starts at a high point on the y-axis at zero kinetic energy. What error have they made?
toLevel4.answer: The curve should start at zero on the y-axis because no particles have zero kinetic energy
distractors: The curve should start at the peak value on the y-axis at zero energy
The curve is correct — it always starts at a high point on the y-axis
The curve should start at the Ea value on the x-axis

toLevel4.stem: A student draws a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve that is perfectly symmetrical like a bell curve. What correction is needed?
toLevel4.answer: The curve should be asymmetric with a longer tail extending to the right
distractors: The curve is correct — Maxwell-Boltzmann curves are always symmetrical
The curve should be symmetrical but wider than drawn
The curve should have a longer tail extending to the left instead

toLevel4.stem: A student labels the x-axis of a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve as 'temperature'. Is this correct?
toLevel4.answer: No — the x-axis should be labelled 'kinetic energy'
distractors: Yes — the x-axis always represents temperature
No — the x-axis should be labelled 'time'
Yes — kinetic energy and temperature are the same thing

toLevel4.stem: A student draws a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve where the right tail touches the x-axis and stops. What should they correct?
toLevel4.answer: The tail should approach but never touch the x-axis, continuing asymptotically
distractors: The tail is correct — it should always touch the x-axis at a specific point
The tail should cross below the x-axis on the right side
The tail should curve upward and continue rising to the right

toLevel4.stem: A student is asked to mark the activation energy on a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve. Where should they place it?
toLevel4.answer: As a vertical line on the x-axis, typically in the tail region of the curve
distractors: At the peak of the curve on the y-axis
At the origin where the curve begins
At the highest point of the curve on the x-axis

toLevel4.stem: A student needs to shade the area representing particles that can react. They should shade:
toLevel4.answer: the area under the curve to the right of the Ea line
distractors: the area under the curve to the left of the Ea line
the entire area under the curve from start to finish
the area above the curve to the right of the peak

toLevel4.stem: A student labels the y-axis as 'number of particles'. A more precise label would be:
toLevel4.answer: proportion of particles with a given kinetic energy
distractors: total kinetic energy of all the particles
rate of reaction at that kinetic energy
temperature of particles at that energy

toLevel4.stem: A correctly drawn Maxwell-Boltzmann curve starts at {{blank:1}} on the y-axis, rises to a peak, and has a tail that extends to the {{blank:2}} without touching the x-axis.
distractors: one
left
the peak
centre

toLevel4.stem: The activation energy is marked as a {{blank:1}} line on the x-axis, and the area to the {{blank:2}} of it represents particles that can react.
distractors: horizontal
left
diagonal
centre

toLevel4.stem: A more precise y-axis label than 'number of particles' is '{{blank:1}} of particles with a given kinetic {{blank:2}}'.
distractors: total
mass

speed

toLevel5.stem: A student draws a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve with the peak very close to the y-axis and a long extended tail. What can be inferred about the temperature?
toLevel5.answer: The temperature is relatively low, as most particles have low kinetic energies
distractors: The temperature is very high, giving particles extreme kinetic energies
The temperature cannot be determined from the shape of the curve
The temperature is at absolute zero, with no particle movement

toLevel5.stem: A student states: 'The average energy of the particles is at the peak of the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve.' Is this correct?
toLevel5.answer: Not exactly — the peak shows the modal (most common) energy, which is slightly less than the mean
distractors: Correct — the peak always represents the average kinetic energy exactly
Incorrect — the average energy is at the far right end of the tail
Correct — mean and mode are always identical on this type of curve

toLevel5.stem: Why is it significant that the curve is asymmetric with a right-skew rather than symmetric?
toLevel5.answer: It shows that a small but important fraction of particles have much higher energy than the mode
distractors: It indicates that most particles have very high energy, not low energy
It is an artifact of how the graph is drawn and has no physical significance
It proves that all particles have exactly the same kinetic energy

toLevel5.stem: A peer claims: 'The area under the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve changes when a catalyst is added.' Evaluate this claim.
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect — the area stays the same because the number of particles and their energies are unchanged
distractors: Correct — the catalyst adds more particles, increasing the area
Correct — the catalyst removes particles, decreasing the area
Incorrect — the area changes only when a catalyst is removed

toLevel5.stem: Two Maxwell-Boltzmann curves are drawn on the same axes. Curve A has a higher, narrower peak positioned further left than Curve B. What can be concluded?
toLevel5.answer: Curve A represents a lower temperature than Curve B
distractors: Curve A represents a higher temperature than Curve B
Curve A has more total particles than Curve B
Curve A has a lower activation energy than Curve B

toLevel5.stem: A student argues: 'Since the curve never touches the x-axis on the right, it means the total area under the curve is infinite.' Evaluate this reasoning.
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect — the tail approaches zero rapidly enough that the total area remains finite and constant
distractors: Correct — the area is technically infinite but we treat it as finite for convenience
Incorrect — the curve does touch the x-axis at a very high kinetic energy value
Correct — this is why the total number of particles cannot be calculated

toLevel5.stem: On a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve, the Ea for a particular reaction falls exactly at the peak. What does this tell us about the reaction?
toLevel5.answer: About half the particles have enough energy to react — this is a relatively easy reaction at this temperature
distractors: No particles can exceed the Ea because the peak is the maximum energy
All particles exceed the Ea because the peak is the most common energy
The reaction cannot occur at all because the Ea equals the modal energy

toLevel5.stem: A student claims that the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution only applies at thermal equilibrium. Is this a valid limitation?
toLevel5.answer: Yes — the distribution assumes particles have had time to reach a steady-state energy distribution
distractors: No — the distribution applies regardless of whether equilibrium has been reached
No — thermal equilibrium has no connection to particle energy distributions
Yes — but only for gaseous systems, not for liquids or solutions
